items.title: 71542_Bill Coleman autobiographical manuscript
items.q: Teddy called three numbers and when he gave the starting beat on the first number... Teddy asked me what was wrong... So Fess told me to take the night off.

ctx.x: I never got angry with him because we were almost like brothers who really loved each other and sometimes I would come home juiced and do the same to him as he did to me.

During the months that Teddy was at the Savoy, an orchestra by the name of the Alabama State College was engaged for a few days. The leader was named Erskine Hawkins and he was the second trumpet player I ever heard that could play altissimo C or C above the high one in the treble clef. The first one was with Jimmie Lunceford whom I heard at the Lafayette shortly after I came back from Europe.

After a few months at the Savoy, Teddy Hill and orchestra were engaged to play at the Ubangi Club which had been Connie's Inn and Harlem Club before. In place of having girls in the line up, there were six female impersonators and the main attraction was a lesbian named Gladys Lentley. Gladys was quite plump and wore a man's full dress suit for her act and dressed like a man except for a skirt when she had on street clothes. Gladys played piano, sang and tap danced a little.
